The customerId Stand-In →

Rewriting the Ticket Service

The in-memory array is gone; the exported functions, and everything above them, aren't.

Figure 2.14 is the whole of ticket.service.js as it stands now — compare it against Lesson 1's in-memory version (Figure 1.9) side by side if you still have that slide open.

// Figure 2.14: Prisma-backed queries (src/services/ticket.service.js)
import prisma from '../config/db.js';

const userSummary = { select: { id: true, name: true, email: true } };

export const getAllTickets = async () =>
  prisma.ticket.findMany({
    orderBy: { id: 'asc' },
    include: { customer: userSummary, assignedAgent: userSummary },
  });

export const getTicketById = async (id) =>
  prisma.ticket.findUnique({
    where: { id },
    include: { customer: userSummary, assignedAgent: userSummary },
  });

export const createTicket = async ({ subject, description, customerId }) =>
  prisma.ticket.create({
    data: { subject, description, customerId },
    include: { customer: userSummary },
  });

Every exported function has the exact same name and the exact same parameters it had in Week 1 — that's the payoff of the services-as-a-layer topic from Lesson 1 arriving for real: not one line of ticket.controller.js needed to change for this rewrite, because it only ever called ticketService.getAllTickets() and so on, never touched the old array directly.

userSummary is a small object reused across all three queries, holding the select from the previous topic's query-methods slide — id, name, email only, deliberately never password. Passed into include, it shapes what each related customer/assignedAgent object actually contains in the response, rather than every column MySQL happens to store for a User row. getAllTickets also adds orderBy: { id: 'asc' } — the in-memory array was always naturally in insertion order; a real database makes no promises about row order unless you ask for one explicitly.
